name: hexagonal
context: Hexagonal Architecture isolates domain logic from external dependencies by structuring applications around inward-pointing dependencies. The core business logic sits at the center, completely independent of databases, web frameworks, or external APIs. External concerns connect through well-defined ports (interfaces) and adapters (implementations).
benefits: Isolated testability: Business logic can be unit-tested in isolation using mock adapters without requiring databases, HTTP servers, or external services
Framework independence: Core domain logic contains no framework annotations or infrastructure dependencies
Swappable adapters: Database, messaging, or external API implementations can be changed without touching domain code
Clean domain model: Business rules written in domain language rather than technical jargon
Maintainability: Changes in one area do not cascade into unrelated areas due to clear boundaries
Technology flexibility: Deployment choices remain open; can start as monolith and migrate to microservices when needed
Test-driven development support: Enables TDD workflow by allowing domain-first development
Reduced regression risk: Framework upgrades stay contained in adapters rather than metastasizing through codebase
tradeoffs: Initial complexity: More interfaces and indirection compared to simpler architectures
Over-engineering risk: May be excessive overhead for simple CRUD applications
Mapping overhead: Data transformation code required between layers (domain objects to/from DTOs)
Learning curve: Requires understanding of ports/adapters pattern and dependency inversion principle
File count increase: More files than layered architecture due to ports, adapters, and conversion code
Ceremony overhead: Small teams may spend more time on architecture than delivering features
use_cases: Domain-driven design projects where ubiquitous language must be reflected in code
Complex business rules that need to be isolated from infrastructure for testing
Applications expected to outlive their initial technology choices
Projects requiring multiple input providers (REST, GraphQL, CLI, message queues)
Systems needing independent deployability of bounded contexts
Applications with significant test coverage requirements
Projects transitioning from monolith to microservices
avoid_when: Simple CRUD operations with straightforward data access patterns
Small teams with simple requirements and tight deadlines
Proof-of-concept or MVP projects where speed is prioritized over maintainability
Applications where the entire value proposition is infrastructure glue (API gateways, data pipelines)
Strong consistency requirements without tolerance for eventual consistency
component_types: Domain (Core): Pure business logic, entities, value objects, domain services, domain events
Application Services: Use cases/command handlers that orchestrate domain objects
Inbound Ports (Driving): Interfaces for incoming operations that drive the application
Outbound Ports (Driven): Interfaces for external dependencies that the application drives
Driving (Primary) Adapters: Entry points that call inbound ports
Driven (Secondary) Adapters: Implementations that fulfill outbound port contracts
Anti-Corruption Layer: Translation layer during migration from legacy systems
technology_stack: Languages: Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C#
Web Frameworks: FastAPI, Spring Boot, Express.js, NestJS, ASP.NET Core
Databases: PostgreSQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB, any database with adapter
Message Brokers: Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS with adapter pattern
Testing: pytest, JUnit, pytest-asyncio, TestContainers for integration tests
DI Containers: Spring DI, Python injector, Dagger (optional but recommended)
anti_patterns: Anemic Domain Model: Migrating structure but leaving business logic scattered in use cases
Leaking Adapters: Allowing framework coupling or infrastructure imports to bleed into domain layer
Port Explosion: Creating one port per method leading to interface proliferation
Fake Hexagonal: Looking like hexagonal architecture but preserving old coupling problems
Over-abstracting: Creating interfaces for everything, not just things that actually change
God Objects: Large domain services that violate single responsibility principle
Package-by-Layer: Organizing by architectural layer instead of feature/bounded context
design_principles: Dependency Rule: All dependencies point from outside to inside. The domain core depends on nothing external. Adapters depend on ports, never the reverse.

Ports Define Needs: Interfaces use domain language exclusively. If an interface mentions 'JPA' or 'HTTP', it's not a port—it's an infrastructure leak. A method called findActiveUsersByRegion() is a good port; executeSQLQuery(String sql) is not.
One Port Per Seam: Define one port per bounded context seam, not one per handler. Keep ports narrow (2-4 methods). This follows the Interface Segregation Principle.
Adapters Implement Ports: Adapters live in the infrastructure layer and contain all framework coupling. The domain never imports from the adapters layer.
Composition Root: Wire all dependencies together in a single place (typically main() or a configuration class). This explicit wiring makes dependencies visible and testable.
Domain Language: Business rules should be expressed in ubiquitous language. The domain model should be readable by domain experts without technical jargon.
No Framework Annotations in Domain: Keep framework annotations (@Entity, @RestController, etc.) in adapters. The domain core should compile without any framework dependencies.
best_practices: Start Domain-First: Design the domain model before thinking about adapters. Let the domain drive the port interfaces.
Keep Ports Narrow: Ports should have 2-4 methods maximum. Large ports indicate too much responsibility and violate single responsibility.
Map Aggressively: Domain ↔ DTO ↔ Entity mappings feel like boilerplate but enable separate evolution. Use MapStruct or similar tools to reduce ceremony.
Test Domain in Milliseconds: Use fake adapters for unit tests. If tests require a database or Spring context, the dependency rule is violated.
Multiple Adapters Per Port: Support REST, GraphQL, CLI, and message consumers through separate driving adapters calling the same inbound port.
Incrementally Migrate: Use the Strangler Fig pattern. Migrate one bounded context at a time while maintaining production stability.
Validate Port Design: If a port mirrors a specific database's API, it hasn't abstracted anything. Ports should describe what the domain needs in domain terms.
